did_you_know.text: Isaiah begins with an invitation to everyone who is thirsty, including those who have no money, to come and receive water, wine, and milk without money and without cost.
The prophet raises a question about wasted resources: Why spend money on what is not bread and labor for what does not satisfy? Instead, he calls people to listen to the Lord and eat what is good.

Listening to the Lord is described as a source of life: “Listen, and your soul will live.” As a result, the Lord promises to make an everlasting covenant and refers to “the faithful mercies shown to David.”
In verses 3–4, a figure is described as one whom the Lord appointed for the peoples as a witness, a leader, and a commander. This highlights the role of leadership with significance beyond Israel.
The chapter describes a future in which nations unknown to Israel will call on it, and nations that did not know it will hasten to it, for the sake of the Lord and the Holy One of Israel.
The call, “Seek the Lord while he may be found,” emphasizes that people should seek the Lord and call on him while he is near.
Repentance is described as abandoning evil ways and thoughts and returning to the Lord. Those who return to the Lord receive mercy, and the chapter emphasizes that he freely forgives.
Isaiah teaches that the Lord’s ways and thoughts are not like human ways and thoughts; the next verse compares this difference to the height of the heavens above the earth.
Rain and snow serve as an illustration of useful action: they water the earth, make it produce growth, and provide seed for the sower and bread for the eater.
Just as water accomplishes its work on the earth, the word of the Lord does not return to him empty. Instead, it accomplishes his purpose and succeeds in the task for which he sent it.
